Must Know

6 concepts
01LLM

LLM is a model that learns from large amounts of text to predict the next token. It can generate, classify and summarize content but does not guarantee the information is always correct.

Further reading

Learn about the LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-tuning & Quantization: AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization

Link to this question
02RAG

RAG retrieves relevant documents and then puts them into context for LLM to respond. Appropriate updated data, source should be cited; Quality depends on both retrieval and generation.

Further reading

Learn about the LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-tuning & Quantization: AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization

Link to this question
03MCP

MCP standardizes how AI applications connect to tools, resources, and prompts through a host-client-server architecture. Authentication, authorization, and action approval remain controlled by the application.

Further reading

Learn about the LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-tuning & Quantization: AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization

Link to this question
04Agent

Agents combine models, tools, states, and control loops to perform multiple steps. Need clear goals, step/cost limits and stopping conditions.

Further reading

Learn about the LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-tuning & Quantization: AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization

Link to this question
05Fine-tuning

Fine-tuning updates weights using task data to improve specific behaviors or abilities. Use when prompt is not enough; Do not substitute retrieval for constantly changing knowledge.

Further reading

Learn about the LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-tuning & Quantization: AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization

Link to this question
06Quantization

Quantization reduces the accuracy of representing weights or activations, for example BF16 to INT8/INT4. Saves memory and can speed up if the hardware supports it; quality deterioration assessment is required.

Further reading

Learn about the LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-tuning & Quantization: AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization

LLM Fundamentals

80 questions
01What are foundation models, and how have they changed AI engineering?

The Foundation model is pre-trained on extensive data and reused for many tasks. AI engineering shifts the focus to adaptation, integration, evaluation and operation instead of training each model from scratch.

Further reading

Explained in this video: AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization

Link to this question
02What is a Large Language Model (LLM), and how does it work?

LLM maps tokens to embedding, processes it using multiple network layers, and then predicts the next token distribution. Generate text by iteratively sampling and appending tokens to the context.

Further reading

Explained in this video: AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization

Link to this question
03Inside ChatGPT: What Happens After You Hit Enter?

Essential flow: encapsulate dialogue and instructions, tokenize, prefill, decode each token, then stream the results. Products can add retrieval, tools and filters; ChatGPT internal details are not fully disclosed.

Further reading

Inside ChatGPT: What Happens After You Hit Enter

Link to this question
04What is the Transformer architecture and how does it work?

The transformer uses attention to combine information between locations and a feed-forward network to transform the representation. Residual, normalization and location information help with deep training, handling order and distance relations.

Further reading

Decoding Transformer Architecture

Link to this question
05What are the key components of the Transformer architecture?

Main components: embedding, positional representation, attention, feed-forward, residual connection, normalization and vocabulary output. The decoder that generates text also uses a causal mask.

Further reading

Decoding Transformer Architecture

Link to this question
06Walk me through what happens, step by step, in one forward pass of a decoder-only Transformer.

Token embedding goes through each block: normalization, creating Q/K/V, attention with causal mask, adding residual, feed-forward and then adding residual. End normalization and LM head generate logits; The exact layout depends on the architecture.

Further reading

Decoding Transformer Architecture

Link to this question
07What is tokenization in LLMs?

Tokenization breaks text into tokens and maps them to IDs. Tokens can be characters, bytes, or word fragments; The number of tokens affects the cost, context, and ability to handle each language.

Further reading

Tokenization in LLMs and Tokenization in Large Language Models (LLMs)

Link to this question
08Explain BPE (Byte Pair Encoding).

BPE starts with small symbols and then repeats common pairs to create vocabulary. When encoding, apply learned aggregation operations; Process rare words using smaller pieces.

Further reading

Byte Pair Encoding

Link to this question
09Explain WordPiece and SentencePiece.

WordPiece selects word fragments according to statistical/likelihood criteria, often distinguishing between consecutive fragments. SentencePiece is a raw text tokenization toolkit, supporting BPE or Unigram; not a single algorithm.

Link to this question
10What is positional encoding, and why is it needed in Transformers?

Attention itself does not know the token order. Positional encoding/embedding or RoPE injects positional information into the model to distinguish strings with the same token but different order.

Further reading

Positional Embeddings in LLMs

Link to this question
11What are embeddings?

Embedding is an arithmetic vector representing a token, sentence, or object. Useful relationships are learned through targeted training; Vector distance only has meaning according to the specific model and task.

Further reading

Embeddings in Machine Learning

Link to this question
12Explain the Query(Q), Key(K), and Value(V) in attention.

A query represents what the current token is looking for; keys determine relevance; values carry the information to aggregate. Attention computes softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V.

Further reading

Math behind Attention - Q, K, and V

Link to this question
13What is self-attention, and how does it work in Transformers?

Self-attention takes Q, K and V from the same string. Each token aggregates the value of positions according to similarity weights, within the allowable mask range.

Further reading

Self Attention in Transformers

Link to this question
14What is Cross Attention in Transformers?

Cross-attention takes query from one string and key/value from another string. For example, the decoder accesses the encoder's representation, or the language model retrieves information from the image.

Further reading

Cross Attention in Transformers

Link to this question
15Why do we scale the dot product attention by √dₖ in the Transformer architecture?

As dₖ increases, the dot product variance usually increases, causing the softmax to saturate and the gradient to become small. Dividing by √dₖ keeps the logits scale more stable, under the assumption that the components have appropriate variances.

Further reading

Math behind √dₖ Scaling Factor in Attention

Link to this question
16What is causal masking?

Causal mask covers future positions with negative infinity before softmax. Thanks to that, the current token only relies on the prefix, matching autoregressive generation when reasoning.

Further reading

Causal Masking in Attention

Link to this question
17What are multi-head attention mechanisms? Why use multiple attention heads?

Multi-head attention learns multiple Q/K/V projections, calculates attention in parallel and then combines the results. Heads can capture different relationships instead of forcing all information through one attention operation.

Further reading

Multi-Head Attention in Transformers

Link to this question
18What are Feed-Forward Networks in LLMs?

The FFN independently transforms the representation at each location by projections and nonlinearities, often expanding and then contracting dimensionally. It adds characteristic transformation capacity after the information exchange step of attention.

Further reading

Feed-Forward Networks in LLMs

Link to this question
19What is Generative AI?

Generative AI learns to distribute data to create new content such as text, photos, audio or code. Model-appropriate output does not necessarily mean it is true or has the right to use.

Further reading

What is Generative AI?

Link to this question
20What is the context window in LLMs, and why does it matter?

Context window is the limit of tokens the model can process in one request, usually including input and generation. It determines the amount of history/documents that can be used and affects memory and latency.

Further reading

Context Window in LLMs

Link to this question
21Why is the context window limited in LLMs?

The limit comes from the KV cache, attention cost, positional representation, and trained length. Extending technical limits does not by itself ensure that the model effectively uses the entire context.

Further reading

Why is the context window limited in LLMs?

Link to this question
22What is temperature in the context of LLMs, and how does it affect output?

Temperature divides logits before softmax: lower values concentrate probability; higher values increase diversity. It controls randomness, not correctness; low temperature can still produce hallucinations.

Further reading

How does Temperature control LLM output?

Link to this question
23Why is the first token slower than the rest in an LLM?

Before the first token, the model needs to process all prompts in the prefill step, adding queue and network time. The following tokens reuse the KV cache and only process the new generation.

Further reading

The First-Token Latency Problem in LLMs

Link to this question
24Explain Top-p (nucleus) sampling and Top-k sampling. How do they differ?

Top-k holds the k highest probability tokens; top-p holds the smallest set with a total probability of reaching p. Top-p adapts to the distribution; both remove the tail before sampling.

Further reading

How do Top-k and Top-p Sampling work?

Link to this question
25Compare greedy decoding, beam search, top-k, top-p, and temperature sampling. When does each fail?

Greedy is susceptible to local selection and repetition; Beam search can favor general or short sentences. Top-k/top-p and temperature increase widely but may result in poor token matching; Choose by evaluation according to the task.

Further reading

How do Top-k and Top-p Sampling work?

Link to this question
26What are logits, and how are they used in text generation?

Logits are unstandardized scores on vocabulary. After adjusting temperature, mask and sampling filter, softmax converts them into probability to choose the next token.

Further reading

Understanding Logits in Machine Learning

Link to this question
27What are stop tokens in LLMs, and how does an LLM know when to stop generating?

A stop token is a special ID the model can generate to indicate the end of a turn or sequence. The system also stops when the token limit is reached, a stop sequence is encountered, or the request is canceled.

Further reading

Stop Tokens in LLMs

Link to this question
28What is the difference between a stop token and a stop sequence?

Stop token is a special token in vocabulary. Stop sequence is an application-specified sequence that can consist of multiple tokens; The backend detects the matching sequence to stop generation.

Further reading

Stop Tokens in LLMs

Link to this question
29What are skip connections (residual connections) in Transformers?

Residual connection adds input x to output F(x): y = x + F(x). It creates gradient paths and holds information, helping to train multi-layer networks more stably.

Further reading

Skip connections (residual connections) in Transformers

Link to this question
30What is the difference between open-source and closed-source LLMs? When would you choose one over the other?

Weighted open model allows for self-hosting and customization; need to check the license because open-weight is not always open-source. Closed APIs are generally easy to operate; Choose based on quality, data rights, latency, and total cost.

Link to this question
31What is the difference between encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder Transformer architectures?

Encoder-only uses two-dimensional context, suitable for representation/classification; decoder-only uses causal attention to generate. Encoder-decoder encodes the input and then generates it via cross-attention, suitable for string conversion tasks.

Further reading

Encoder vs Decoder in Transformers

Link to this question
32What is KV cache, and how does it speed up inference?

KV cache stores the key/value of the processed token at each layer. When generating new tokens, reuse the cache instead of recalculating the entire prefix; Trade speed for memory that increases with length.

Further reading

What is KV Cache in LLMs?

Link to this question
33Estimate the KV cache memory needed to serve a large model. How does it constrain batch size and context length?

KV memory is approximately 2 × layers × batch × tokens × KV_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_value. It grows linearly with batch size and context length; reserve VRAM for weights, activations, workspace and allocator overhead.

Further reading

KV Cache Compression

Link to this question
34KV Cache Compression

KV compression can use quantization, head sharing, selective token retention or cache compression architecture. The trade-off is precision, long recall, and decompression cost; Need to measure on actual long tasks.

Further reading

KV Cache Compression

Link to this question
35What is model distillation, and how is it used with LLMs?

Distillation trains students to learn the teacher's output, distribution, or processing traces. Reduce inference cost; student may lose capacity if its architecture or data are not sufficiently representative.

Further reading

How does Knowledge Distillation work?

Link to this question
36What is Mixture of Experts (MoE), and how does it work in models like Mixtral?

MoE has many experts and the router chooses several experts for each token. The total parameters are large but only partially activated; still need expert memory and load balancing/communication handling.

Further reading

Mixture of Experts Explained

Link to this question
37What is the difference between dense and sparse models?

Dense activates the majority of parameters for each token; sparse, like MoE, only activates a subset. Sparse saves compute per token but has additional routing, memory, and load distribution costs.

Further reading

Mixture of Experts Explained

Link to this question
38How does DeepSeek-V4 work?

DeepSeek-V4 combines MoE with hybrid CSA/HCA attention to compress and access long KV histories efficiently, alongside a local sliding-window branch. mHC changes residual connections, aiming to preserve capability while reducing long-context cost.

Further reading

DeepSeek-V4 Architecture Explained

Transformers: DeepSeek-V4

Link to this question
39What is Flash Attention?

FlashAttention computes exact attention in tiles, minimizing data transfers between SRAM and HBM without materializing the full attention matrix. It reduces intermediate memory and IO; dense attention still has quadratic arithmetic complexity in sequence length.

Further reading

Decoding Flash Attention in LLMs

Link to this question
40What is Cross-Entropy Loss?

Cross-entropy measures the level at which the model assigns probability to the correct label/token: for a label is -log p(correct token). Next-token training averages this loss across loss-weighted positions.

Further reading

Math Behind Cross-Entropy Loss

Link to this question
41What is Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), and how does it differ from Multi-Head Attention (MHA)?

GQA divides query heads into groups that share a key/value head. It reduces KV cache size compared to MHA; MQA is the case where there is only one KV head for every query head.

Further reading

Grouped Query Attention

Link to this question
42How does Sliding Window Attention work?

Sliding-window attention only looks at a token area near the current location. Reduce compute/cache by window but may lose long-distance relationships; Multiple layers or global branches help spread information more widely.

Further reading

How does Sliding Window Attention work?

Link to this question
43How do Attention Sinks work?

Attention sink is a position that receives a lot of attention even though the content is not important, usually at the beginning of the chain. Keeping a few sink tokens close to the window can help keep streaming stable; Sink should not be considered semantic evidence.

Further reading

How do Attention Sinks work?

Link to this question
44How does Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) work, and why is it preferred over learned positional embeddings?

RoPE rotates the Q/K component pairs according to position, making the dot product dependent on relative position. No need for a separate study position embedding table; Extrapolating long contexts still requires appropriate techniques and validation.

Further reading

Math Behind RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding)

Link to this question
45Explain Layer Normalization

LayerNorm normalizes the characteristic dimensions of each token by mean and variance, then applies the learned scale/bias. It stabilizes activation magnitude, independent of batch size.

Further reading

Batch Normalization vs Layer Normalization

Link to this question
46Explain RMSNorm (Root Mean Square Layer Normalization)

RMSNorm divides the vector by the root mean square and then multiplies the learned scale. Does not subtract mean like LayerNorm, so it is simpler and often reduces some computational costs.

Further reading

RMSNorm (Root Mean Square Layer Normalization)

Link to this question
47Why do modern Transformers use Pre-LayerNorm (Pre-Norm) instead of Post-LayerNorm?

Pre-Norm normalizes before attention/FFN, keeping the residual curve favorable for the gradient in the deep network. Post-Norm normalization after addition; Stability also depends on initialization, optimizer and architecture.

Further reading

RMSNorm (Root Mean Square Layer Normalization)

Link to this question
48What are scaling laws (Chinchilla), and how do they guide model size vs training data decisions?

Scaling laws relate loss to parameters, data, and compute. Chinchilla shows that under a fixed training budget it is necessary to balance the model with the amount of tokens; The optimal ratio also changes if long-term service costs are considered.

Link to this question
49Your LLM keeps ignoring your instructions. How do you make it follow structured output formats?

Use a constrained schema if the backend supports it, the examples are valid, and the instructions do not conflict. Validate syntax and operations in the application; Limited retry and clear error return when not responding.

Link to this question
50Your LLM-powered tool hits the context window limit on long documents. How do you handle it?

Split documents, retrieve related parts or process them hierarchically and then synthesize. Leave output budget, keep source/ID through steps; Only switch to long context when the quality benefits justify the cost.

Link to this question
51Your LLM does not admit when it does not know the answer. How do you make it say "I don't know"?

Train/give examples for situations where evidence is lacking, adding retrieval and denial rules. Adjusting the threshold with eval has unanswerable questions; Do not rely on self-declared model confidence.

Link to this question
52Your LLM generates responses that are too verbose. How do you control response length?

State the limit on the number of ideas, length and desired output examples; The token limit is only the final barrier because it can cut the sentence in half. Measure the rate at which requirements are met while retaining sufficient information.

Link to this question
53Your LLM memorized proprietary training data and leaks it in responses. How do you prevent this?

Remove or de-identify sensitive data before training, limit access, and test data extraction. With a leaked model, isolate/rollback and then retrain or unlearn has been verified; The output filter is not secure enough.

Link to this question
54Your LLM coding assistant generates outdated code using deprecated libraries. How do you fix it?

Pin the library version, bring the current documentation/API into context, and run the test/lint in a live environment. Verify the function name using the tool; Don't just ask the model to remember the new version.

Link to this question
55Your tokenizer splits important domain terms into meaningless subword pieces. How do you fix it?

First measure the actual impact on token budget and quality. Can use specialized data, change tokenizer/model; Adding new tokens requires related embedding training, not just editing the vocabulary list.

Link to this question
56Your Transformer's KV cache grows too large during long sequence generation. How do you manage memory?

Limit context and batch, use GQA/MQA or quantized KV when supported; sliding window/eviction needs to evaluate information loss. PagedAttention reduces allocation fragmentation, but does not itself reduce the number of useful KV bytes.

Further reading

Paged Attention in LLMs

Link to this question
57Your Transformer runs out of memory on long documents due to quadratic self-attention. How do you scale it?

Use FlashAttention to reduce intermediate memory, chunking/retrieval or sparse/sliding-window architecture for very long strings. Reduce batches and use checkpointing when training; Distinguish activation memory from KV cache.

Further reading

How does Sliding Window Attention work? and Decoding Flash Attention in LLMs

Link to this question
58Your distilled student model fails on the complex reasoning that the teacher model handled. How do you close the gap?

Added difficult task data, verified solution steps and easy to difficult curriculum. Increase student capacity if necessary; Compare teacher/student errors and avoid distilling questions that teacher answers incorrectly.

Link to this question
59After RLHF alignment, your LLM became safer but lost capability on hard tasks. How do you manage the alignment tax?

Measure safety and capacity for each task group, adjust preference data and regularization/KL intensity. Mix capacity data and choose checkpoints on both criteria instead of optimizing a total safety score.

Link to this question
60Your RLHF-trained LLM is gaming the reward model instead of being genuinely helpful. How do you fix reward hacking?

Find high reward but low quality examples, edit the rubric/data and check with independent judges or humans. Limit the optimal reward level, add regularization and keep eval out of the reward model.

Further reading

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)

Link to this question
61Your chatbot loses context after 10 turns in a conversation. How do you maintain a long conversation context?

Keep turns close, summarize status, and retrieve relevant memories. Save important events with source and privacy; Do not connect infinitely every time because it wastes context and increases noise.

Further reading

AI Agent Memory

Link to this question
62Your chatbot fails when users switch topics mid-conversation. How do you handle topic switches?

Track topics/intent and separate status by task; Retrieve only relevant history. When changing an unclear topic, ask for clarification instead of dragging over all the assumptions of the previous task.

Link to this question
63Your QA system always generates an answer even when no answer exists in the context. How do you detect unanswerable questions?

Evaluate answerability from the evidence and allow abstain. Check question coverage, cite each conclusion, and use an eval set of sentences without answers in context.

Link to this question
64Your summarization system hallucinated facts not in the original article. How do you fix it?

Summarize according to the evidence, keep separate figures/names attached to the source paragraph and check each important statement. Detail type not supported by source; with ambiguous information, keeping the original's level of uncertainty.

Link to this question
65Your text generation repeats phrases in long outputs. How do you fix repetition?

Check prompt/history for repetition, stop condition and sampling. Can adjust repetition penalty or loop detection; evaluated to not penalize terms that force repetition in code or data.

Link to this question
66Transformers work on text, so can they also understand images?

Yes. Vision Transformer divides the image into patches and then processes it with the Transformer; VLM connects the vision encoder to the language model via projector or cross-attention. Need training data for image and language association.

Further reading

Decoding Vision Transformer (ViT)

Link to this question
67Small Language Models (SLMs)

SLM is a relatively small language model, suitable for low latency, limited devices, or narrow tasks. Choose eval, because fewer parameters does not by itself guarantee better quality and cost in any case.

Further reading

Small Language Models (SLMs)

Link to this question
68Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)

LRM is optimized for multi-step inference and often uses additional compute during inference. Can solve difficult tasks better but slower/more token-consuming; need to limit budget and verify results.

Further reading

Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)

Link to this question
69Jev and System One Models

Jev is a System One model for decisions like: choosing answers, scoring rubrics or estimating probabilities, instead of generating free text. Suitable for routing/fast checking; It is still necessary to calibrate the threshold according to actual data.

Further reading

Jev and System One Models Explained

70What are Autoregressive Models?

The autoregressive model decomposes the sequence probability into the probability of each element conditional on the prefix. Sequential generation by predicting the next element and appending it to the history.

Further reading

Autoregressive Models

Link to this question
71Explain the difference between autoregressive and masked language modeling.

Autoregressive learning predicts the next token with causal context, conveniently generating text. Masked language modeling recovers masked tokens from a two-dimensional context, often using representation learning such as BERT.

Link to this question
72Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)

PPO is a policy-gradient algorithm that limits the level of policy changes by a clipped surrogate target. In RLHF, it optimizes reward and often adds KL with reference policy to avoid too strong deviation.

Further reading

Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)

Link to this question
73Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)

The DPO learns directly from the liked/disliked response pair using the objective with the referenced policy. There is no need to train a separate reward model or RL rollout round like PPO in the standard DPO formula.

Further reading

Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)

Link to this question
74Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)

GRPO takes multiple responses to the same prompt, calculates relative superiority in the group and then updates the policy. It avoids separate criticism/value models; Quality depends on reward and sample group diversity.

Further reading

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)

Link to this question
75Recursive Language Models (RLMs)

RLM considers long prompts as data in the external environment, tells the model to write operations to read/split and call recursively on the parts. This is an inference strategy, not simply increasing the context window.

Further reading

Recursive Language Models (RLMs)

Recursive Language Models

76Continual Learning in LLMs

Continuous learning updates the model through new batches of data/tasks while trying to maintain old capabilities. Use replay, regularization or adapter; Evaluate both new data and previous performance test sets.

Further reading

Continual Learning in LLMs

Link to this question
77What is Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI)?

RSI is the idea that the system improves the process/model itself creating the possibility for further improvement. Need to measure independent benefits, resource limitations and change control; This process cannot be automatically accelerated indefinitely.

Further reading

What is Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI)?

Link to this question
78How do Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) work?

Diffusion language model learns to recover strings from noisy states or masked tokens through multiple steps. Multiple locations can be updated at the same time; Speed/quality depends on denoise schedule and architecture, not automatically faster than autoregressive.

Further reading

How do Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) work?

Link to this question
79How Does LLM Watermarking Work?

Watermark text that creates a keyed statistical bias in the token selection for later inspection by the detector. Paraphrase and short text reduce credibility; need to measure false positives, do not consider findings as absolute proof.

Further reading

How Does LLM Watermarking Work?

Link to this question
80How do RNNs and Transformers differ?

RNN processes states sequentially, is difficult to parallelize over time, and easily loses long-distance relationships. Transformer uses attention to link positions directly, parallelizing training better but attention/cache can consume memory.

Further reading

How do RNNs and Transformers differ?

Prompt Engineering

30 questions
01What is prompt engineering, and why is it critical for AI applications?

Prompt engineering designs instructions, context, examples, and output formats so that the model performs the task correctly. It directly affects quality, cost and testability, but does not replace backend control.

Link to this question
02Explain zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting with examples.

Zero-shot: stating classification requirements without examples; one-shot: add a sample; few-shot: add a few representative samples. Choose examples with label boundaries and hard cases, not just similar samples.

Further reading

Explain zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting with examples

Link to this question
03What is chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, and when should you use it?

CoT encourages multi-step solving, useful for math or structured reasoning. Not guaranteed correct; With a reasoning model, you should prioritize the goal and verify the answer, not by default requiring all internal thinking to be made public.

Further reading

How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting work?

Link to this question
04Explain self-consistency prompting and how it improves reasoning.

Generate multiple independent solutions and then synthesize the answers, often by voting, to reduce the error of a line of reasoning. Increases costs and doesn't help much if the models have the same systematic error.

Link to this question
05What is tree-of-thought prompting?

Tree-of-thought extends multiple solutions, evaluates intermediate states, and chooses which branch to continue/backtrack from. Useful when structured searches are needed; Need budget and reliable status criteria.

Further reading

How does Tree of Thoughts work?

Link to this question
06What is ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) prompting, and how does it work?

ReAct interleaves action selection with tool execution and observation reception. The application controls the loop, validates tool calls and stop conditions; The solution must be based on real tool results.

Further reading

ReAct Agent

Link to this question
07What is a system prompt, and how does it influence model behavior?

System prompt sets roles, rules, and constraints as high priority in the conversation. It affects behavior but is not a secret place or security boundary against all prompt injection.

Link to this question
08How do you structure prompts for consistent structured output (JSON, XML)?

Specify the schema, data types, required fields and how to represent missing data; Use constrained output if supported. Parse, validate schema and check business before use; Limit the number of edits/retries.

Link to this question
09What is prompt injection, and how do you defend against it?

Prompt injection is an untrusted instruction that attempts to override the system's target. Separate data from instructions, limit permissions/tools, validate parameters, and control actions outside the model.

Further reading

Prompt Injection in LLMs

OWASP: Prompt Injection

Link to this question
10What is jailbreaking in LLMs, and what are common jailbreak techniques?

Jailbreaks attempt to circumvent the policy by role-switching, context camouflage, encryption, or multiple exploits. Defend with counter-testing, policy enforcement, and impact limiting, not just keyword blacklisting.

Further reading

Prompt Injection in LLMs

Link to this question
11How do you optimize prompts for cost and latency?

Remove redundant context, choose valid examples, limit output, and use cache prefixes when appropriate. Measure quality, TTFT and cost on successful tasks before shortening or changing models.

Link to this question
12What is the difference between prompt engineering and prompt tuning?

Prompt engineering changes the input text without updating the weights. Prompt tuning learns prompt vectors continuously using gradients, often freezing the background model; need data and training.

01What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and why is it important?

RAG finds relevant documents and then puts the evidence into context for the model to answer. It helps update knowledge and extract sources without retraining; does not eliminate hallucination on its own.

01What is an AI agent, and how does it differ from a simple LLM call?

Fine-Tuning and Model Adaptation

32 questions
01What is fine-tuning, and when should you fine-tune an LLM?

Fine-tuning continues to train the weights on the target data. Used to improve behavior/format/task stability when prompt and retrieval are not enough, and have reliable data and eval.

Further reading

Explained in this video: AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization

Link to this question
02Explain the difference between full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT).

Full fine-tuning updates all parameters, flexible but consumes memory/compute. PEFT only learns a fraction of what adapter/LoRA does, is cheaper and easier to manage but may limit adaptation.

Further reading

Explained in this video: AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization

Link to this question
03What is LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation), and how does it work?

LoRA freezes W and learns low-rank updates ΔW = BA. The number of parameters decreases when the rank is small; Adapters can be served separately or included in the weighting as the architecture/number model allows.

Further reading

Explained in this video: AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization

Link to this question
04What is QLoRA, and how does it enable fine-tuning on consumer hardware?

QLoRA holds the quantized base model, typically 4-bit, and then learns the LoRA adapter with calculations at appropriate precision. Reduce weight memory; activation, gradient and optimizer still take up significant VRAM.

Further reading

Explained in this video: AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization

Link to this question
05How does fine-tuning work?

Prepare data and loss mask, forward calculates loss, backprop calculates gradient and then the optimizer updates the opened parameters. Monitor validation, save checkpoints, and test for performance degradation before deployment.

Further reading

How does fine-tuning work?

Link to this question
06Explain Prefix Tuning and Prompt Tuning. How are they different from LoRA?

Prompt tuning learns the prompt vector at input; prefix tuning learns prefix states, often affecting multiple layers of attention. LoRA learns low-rank updates for weight matrices; All three usually keep the base model fixed.

Further reading

How does Prefix Tuning work?

Link to this question
07What is adapter-based fine-tuning?

Adapter-based tuning inserts small modules with learned parameters into the network, freezing most of the base model. Each task can use its own adapter; Adding modules can increase latency if they cannot be merged.

Further reading

Explained in this video: AI Engineering Explained: LLM, RAG, MCP, Agent, Fine-Tuning, Quantization

Link to this question
08Explain the difference between pre-training, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and preference optimization (RLHF/DPO).

Pre-training learns from extensive data; SFT learns the desired response by example; preference optimization adjusts according to choice/reward. They address different goals and are often combined in stages.

Further reading

Decoding InstructGPT

Link to this question
09What is RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback), and how is it used to align LLMs?

RLHF collects human preferences, often learns the reward model and then optimizes the policy using RL with regularization. The goal is useful/appropriate behavior; Biased preferences or wrong rewards can lead to reward hacking.

Further reading

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)

Link to this question
10What is Deep RL from Human Preferences, the paper that started RLHF?

The Deep RL from Human Preferences work learns reward from comparing segments of human-rated behavior. Agents use learned rewards to optimize policies, reducing the need to handwrite the full reward function.

Further reading

Deep RL from Human Preferences

Link to this question
11Why did DPO displace PPO-based RLHF at many labs? When is online RL still better?

DPO simplifies the pipeline because it learns from offline preferences, without needing a separate critique/reward model in the standard formula. Online RL is useful when it comes to discovering new behavior and having a reliable reward/verifier; DPO does not replace every situation.

12What is instruction tuning, and why is it important for chat models?

Instruction tuning is SFT on diverse instruction-response pairs so that the model knows what to do as requested. It improves interactivity but does not by itself guarantee factuality, safety or usability of the tool.

Collect data properly, have usage rights, consistently label and eliminate errors/duplicates/PII. Split train/validation/test to avoid source leaks, standardize chat templates and check length/label distribution.

14What is catastrophic forgetting, and how do you prevent it during fine-tuning?

Catastrophic forgetting is the loss of old abilities when learning new tasks. Reduce learning rate, use PEFT, mix old data/replay or regularization; Measure general capacity eval in parallel with new tasks.

17What is synthetic data generation, and how do you use it for fine-tuning?

Synthetic data is data created by model or simulation, used to expand rare examples/cases. Filter and verify labels/answers, control diversity and keep tests independent to avoid repeating teacher errors.

18What are the key hyperparameters for fine-tuning (learning rate, epochs, batch size, LoRA rank)?

Learning rate determines the update size; epochs is the number of passes through the data; batch gradient/memory noise effects; LoRA rank is the adapter capacity. Choose by validation and budget, there is no universal optimal configuration.

19Do the GPU memory math for full fine-tuning a 7B model in bf16 with Adam. Now with LoRA and QLoRA.

For 7B parameters, bf16 weights and gradients plus two fp32 Adam moments need about 84 GB; fp32 master weights raise this to about 112 GB, excluding activations/workspace. LoRA retains roughly 14 GB of base weights; QLoRA reduces the theoretical base to 3.5 GB, plus metadata and training memory.

20How do you fine-tune a model for a specific domain (legal, medical, finance)?

21What is continual pre-training, and when would you use it?

Continuous pre-training continues the language objective on the new corpus to learn domain distribution/terminology. Suitable when there are many unlabeled documents; then usually requires SFT and a forgetting test.

22How do you merge multiple LoRA adapters?

LoRA updates can be added together with weights or using a merge technique with collision handling. Needs the same base/shape and appropriate scale; validate each task because merge does not preserve the quality of each adapter.

SFT learns from the target response provided by the data; Alignment training directs behavior according to preferences, rewards, or principles. SFT can be partly aligned; alignment is not specific to RLHF.

RLAIF uses AI-generated feedback to learn preferences/rewards instead of human ratings. Expansion is cheaper but inherits judge bias, so it needs to be calibrated with human data and independent testing.

Vector Databases and Embeddings

26 questions
01What are embeddings in the context of AI engineering?

Embedding turns data into learned vectors for search, clustering, recommendation, or classification. It represents the relationship according to the training objective, not a full encoding of all meanings.

Further reading

Embeddings in Machine Learning

Link to this question
02How do embedding models convert text to vectors?

Tokenizer converts text into tokens; The encoder creates hidden states and then pools/projects the sentence/paragraph vector. Query and document must use the same embedding space and the correct model input instructions.

Further reading

What are Embeddings?

Link to this question
03What is Contrastive Learning, and how is it used to train embedding models?

Contrastive learning pulls related pairs close together, pushes unrelated pairs apart with loss like InfoNCE. Hard negatives help distinguish cases of close meaning but wrong answers; Wrong labels can reduce quality.

Further reading

What is Contrastive Learning?

Link to this question
04What is the difference between sparse and dense embeddings?

Sparse vectors have many zero elements, are often associated with words/features, and are strong at exact matching. Dense vector shorter,semantic learning; Hybrid combines to take advantage of two strengths.

Link to this question
05Explain cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance for vector search.

Cosine measures angle: dot(x,y)/(||x||||y||); dot product also depends on the magnitude; Euclidean measures geometric distances. With the L2 normalization vector, the three rankings have appropriate equivalence relations; Always use the metric model trained for.

Further reading

How does a Vector Database work?

Link to this question
06What is a vector database, and how does it differ from a traditional database?

Optimized vector database for storing/querying closest vectors, ANN and metadata filtering. Traditional databases are strong in transactions/relations; Many systems today support both, so choose based on workload instead of product label.

Further reading

How does a Vector Database work?

Link to this question
07How does Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search work?

ANN finds close neighbors with approximate accuracy using graph, partition or quantization instead of full scan. Exchange partial recall for better latency/memory; need to compare with ground truth exact search.

Further reading

How does Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search work?

Link to this question
08Compare HNSW, IVF, and flat indexes. How do you pick one, and what does recall@k cost in latency?

Flat searches accurately but scans a lot; HNSW is fast and often consumes RAM; IVF narrows to clusters. Increasing efSearch/nprobe often increases both recall and latency; Choose by actual size, update and filter.

Further reading

How does Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search work?

Link to this question
09How does an Embedding Cache work?

Embedding cache stores vectors by keys including standardized content, model/version and configuration. Cache hit avoids re-encoding; Need TTL/eviction, authorization and invalidate when model or preprocessor rules change.

Further reading

How does an Embedding Cache work?

Link to this question
10How do you choose the right embedding model for your use case?

Evaluate on query-document pair of domain, language and actual length. Balance recall/nDCG, speed, vector size, license and servicing costs; Don't choose just because the vector is longer.

Link to this question
11What is embedding dimensionality, and how does it affect performance and cost?

Dimensionality is the number of vector components; Increasing dimension usually increases capacity and distance/index cost. Height does not guarantee betterment; dimensionality reduction only if the model supports or has evaluated the transformation.

Link to this question
12How do you handle embedding drift when the embedding model is updated?

Do not mix vectors from two models into the same space even if they have the same number of dimensions. Create new index, re-embed document, run shadow/dual query, pass alias after eval and keep rollback capability.

Link to this question
13What are multi-modal embeddings, and how are they generated?

Multimodal embedding places data types into compatible spaces using associative training, such as image-caption pairs. Query text can find images; Not all image/text encoders are compatible with each other.

Further reading

Multimodal AI

14How do you index and query multi-tenant data in a vector database?

Attach tenant/ACL to metadata and require filtering on the server; Isolate index/collection when needed. Cache and query key must contain permission scope; benchmark recall with real filters.

Link to this question
15What is quantization of embeddings, and how does it reduce storage costs?

Quantization of vector representation in fewer bits or burst codes like PQ to reduce RAM/disk. It causes distance errors; You can use the original vector to rerank the top candidates and measure the recall reduction.

Link to this question
16How do you benchmark and evaluate embedding model quality?

Use a query set with relevance labels, calculate recall@k, MRR or nDCG along with latency/cost. Compared to baseline lexical and exact vector search; reports by language, query group, and document type.

Metadata stores source, ID, tenant, ACL, time, version and document type. It supports filtering, updating/deleting, quoting, and auditing; must be synchronized with the vector instead of being stored externally without control.

Partition/shard, ANN and compression help reduce search/memory scope. Use hot-cold floors, small reranks and fan-out/network evaluation; Make sure the tenant filter does not perform a full system scan.

19What is hybrid search (combining keyword search with vector search)?

Hybrid search runs lexical and vector retrieval and then merges using RRF or calibrated weights. Useful for both proper names/product codes and semantic expressions; need to dedupe and check the final ranking.

Fine-tune with related query-document pairs and quality negatives, especially hard negatives in the right domain. Separate testing to avoid leakage and re-embed the warehouse when changing models; compared to pre-implementation baseline.

25You deployed a new embedding model, and search quality crashed overnight. How do you handle embedding drift?

Rollback the encoder/index to the compatible pair, determining if there is version mixing or incorrect preprocessing. Rebuild new index, shadow evaluation and gradual migration; Track relevance by query group.

26Your semantic search fails for short queries. How do you improve it?

Use hybrid lexical search, query expansion with glossary/context, and clarify intent when needed. Train/eval with really short queries; Avoid over-extension that changes the user's mind.

01How does Prompt Caching work?

33What are TTFT, TPOT, and throughput, and how do they trade against each other?

TTFT is the time to the first token; TPOT is the time each token outputs; throughput is the amount of tokens/requests processed over time. Large batches increase throughput but can increase latency and TPOT; need to lock in optimal SLO first.

Further reading

Prefill vs Decode: LLM Inference Optimization

Link to this question
34How do you monitor and profile LLM inference in production (TTFT, inter-token latency, GPU utilization)?

Record queue/prefill/decode time, TTFT/TPOT by distribution, token length, KV usage, utilization and bandwidth. Use profiler for kernel/communication; High utilization does not mean the request reaches the target latency.

Link to this question
35What is model routing at the infrastructure level, and how do you route requests based on complexity and cost?

The router selects workers/models based on difficulty, budget, capabilities, and cache locality. Use rules/classifier with eval, fallback and load limit; Routing is cheap but incorrect routing can increase retries and overall costs.

Further reading

LLM Routing

Behavioral and Scenario-Based Questions

22 questions
01What is AI Engineering, and how does it differ from Machine Learning Engineering?

AI engineering focuses on turning AI capabilities into products: data, orchestration, evaluation and operations. ML engineering often goes deep into the model/training/serving lifecycle; Boundaries overlap depending on the organization.

Link to this question
02How do you decide whether a problem needs AI or a traditional software solution?

Start request and deterministic baseline. Use AI when input is ambiguous/diverse or pattern learning produces measurable benefits, and errors are acceptable; Choose traditional rules/software when the logic is clear and absolute accuracy is needed.

Link to this question
03How do you measure the ROI of an AI feature?

Measure the revenue increase/time reduction/error reduction benefit compared to the baseline, minus all implementation and operating costs. Use A-B or appropriate measurement design; including reviews, retries and losses due to errors.

Link to this question
04How do you handle hallucinations when they occur in a production AI system?

Reduce impact now, keep trace and identify errors at source/retrieval/model/policy. Fix cause, add eval and limited rollout; Notify affected people when appropriate instead of just fixing silent output.

Link to this question
05How do you decide between using an LLM API vs self-hosting an open-source model?

Compare equivalent quality, data residency/privacy, latency, volume, total cost and operating capacity. API accommodates fluctuating load; self-host is suitable for deep control/high utilization; pre-commit benchmark.

Link to this question
06How do you manage stakeholder expectations for AI projects?

Unify use cases, success criteria and limitations with demo/real cases. Report quality by group with uncertainty, roll out milestones and explain how to handle wrong models.

Link to this question
07Describe your approach to debugging a poor-performing RAG system.

Reproduce query errors, check parser/chunk and measure retrieval recall first. See last context, rerank, prompt and citations; correct stage and add cases to regression instead of unconditionally increasing top-k.

Link to this question
08How do you stay current with the rapidly evolving AI landscape?

Monitor main documents/papers, select changes related to workload and small tests with eval. Document conditions, benefits and limitations; Don't change your stack just because of a new benchmark.

Link to this question
09How do you balance innovation with reliability in AI systems?

Maintain a reliable baseline, test improvements after feature flag with test/risk gate. Only expand when user benefits are measurable and have observability/rollback, without sacrificing required control.

Link to this question
10Tell me about a challenging AI project you worked on. What was the problem? What approach did you take? What trade-offs did you make? What was the outcome?

Answer with real projects according to STAR: context, goals, your decisions, trade-offs, evidenced results and lessons. Do not fabricate data or take credit for someone else's work; State how to measure when exact numbers are not available.

Link to this question
11How would you handle a situation where an AI model produces biased or harmful outputs in production?

Stop/limit the harmful flow, assess the impact and bring the case to the responsible person. Data group investigation, root correction, independent testing, and post-rollout tracking; keep the appeal line.

Link to this question
12How do you approach cost optimization for an AI system that's exceeding budget?

Decompose costs by stage and successful task, identify context/retry/model/traffic causing increase. Try caching, routing and reducing excess tokens via eval; Take into account the cost of moderation and errors before choosing the optimal one.

Link to this question
13Describe a time when you had to choose between model accuracy and latency. How did you make the decision?

Use a real situation: state the SLO, measured options and minimum quality threshold. Explain why the point on the trade-off line was chosen and the results after the rollout; Don't make up experiences if you've only done testing.

Link to this question
14How would you handle a situation where your AI system's quality degrades over time?

Compare versions, input drift, data sources and feedback by group to find the cause. Rollback as needed, add new labels/evals, update pipelines/models, and redeploy with control.

15How do you communicate AI limitations to non-technical stakeholders?

Using a success/failure example, explain the prediction model in terms of sample, with no guarantee of truth. Speaking in terms of business impact, scope of use and route of transfer of people; Avoid covering limits with terminology.

Start with stock models, few-shot or RAG, get specialist labels for critical cases. Use validated active learning/synthetics to scale, keep tests real, and prioritize changes with measurable benefits.
